content_metadata.description: A documentary exploring the making of 'Beetlejuice' in East Corinth, featuring insights from local residents and the film's crew.

qAndA.answer: She asked about making a movie, which was very unusual for the small town of East Corinth.
qAndA.question: What was the unusual request that the woman made when she knocked on Sarah Williams Polli's mother's door?

qAndA.answer: Cheryl Carasik, the set decorator, explains that the town's simple buildings and easy-to-navigate landscape made it ideal for filming.
qAndA.question: Why was East Corinth chosen as a filming location for 'Beetlejuice'?

qAndA.answer: The creek below the bridge was too shallow for the car to land safely, so the crew had to repeatedly build a dam with concrete blocks to raise the water level. This was made even more difficult by storms that washed away their work.
qAndA.question: What was the major challenge faced by the crew when filming the covered bridge scene, and how did they solve it?

qAndA.answer: Cheryl Carasik recalls that the machine was purely for visual effect; it simply dug up dirt and spit it out, creating an animated and 'Tim Burton-esque' visual.
qAndA.question: What was unique about the 'dirt machine' used in one of the scenes?

qAndA.answer: The film was nominated for an Oscar for makeup, which surprised and delighted Ve Neill and Steve LaPorte, who had initially been unsure about the movie's reception.
qAndA.question: What awards recognition did 'Beetlejuice' receive, and how did the makeup artists react?

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: It all started when a lady knocked on the door when my mother was living here and she
was having making dinner for two friends and a woman came to the door and started asking
about a movie which surprised all three of them, nothing like that happens in East Corinth.
And my mother really didn't know what to say and she finally said, would you like a piece
of pie?
The location I think, you know, worked so well and was chosen because of the simplicity
of the buildings and it was easy to kind of get around with camera.
The river for the bridge, everything seemed to work pretty well together and then on the
hill we built the facade of the modern house.
Oh, there was a lot of buzz in the community, a lot of excitement.
Some people weren't happy, they were a little nervous about what all these Hollywood types
would do in a small town like this but the crew was wonderful.
We had research on little towns through New England so for the signage and stuff we
tried to kind of make that go and same with the bridge.
We looked at a bunch of different covered bridges but we had our own issues with that so we
had to make a course of the car could fall through it and whatever and the big thing was
with the covered bridge was we had to block off the creek because below the bridge was
a tiny little creek and we needed at least three or four feet of water for the car to land
and actually get under the water.
So we constantly were blocking this little creek with these one ton blocks of concrete
and we get the water level up to five or six feet and then a big storm had come through
and it would wash them all out and we have to come back.
We did at least three times before we finally shot the movie.
That was probably the biggest thing that made everybody crazy.
I remember the machine, you know, the dirt.
That was the greatest machine.
It did nothing.
It just dug dirt up and spitted out the back.
It was just animated.
You know, it was very Tim Burton.
I mean Tim really hadn't done anything.
He had done, you know, a PB's big adventure and a couple of little Disney shorts that he,
you know, a couple little shorts that he did.
But it was such a weird movie.
We also had, this movie is going to be so weird.
I wonder, I hope people go see it because it's going to be kind of fun and kooky but we
really had no idea how big it was going to be.
I mean, the fact that we got nominated for an Oscar totally blew my mind.
I'll tell you that myself.
I was like, whoa, you know.
We were in good company too.
Yeah.
